prompt.context: The Head of Strategy of Amazon (ecommerce retailer) wants to hire us to address the following issue: 'It's been almost a decade since we launched Amazon Prime in 2005, a subscription service that provides free 2-day shipping to customers for an annual fee. The CEO wants to know 1) how profitable the program has been and 2) what changes should be made going forward to increase profitability.'
prompt.question: The team asks you to take a first crack at the APPROACH (not the answer). Present your structured approach to: 1) evaluating the profitability of the Amazon Prime program, and 2) identifying ways to improve its profitability. You have 30 minutes to prepare and then present to the panel for approximately 15 minutes. A whiteboard will be available; you may bring notes.

clarifying_info.q: Should we consider other Amazon services like Subscribe & Save or Amazon Student?
clarifying_info.a: No, focus on the core Amazon Prime free 2-day shipping program only.

clarifying_info.q: What time period should we analyze?
clarifying_info.a: The program has been running since 2005, so approximately a decade of data is available.

framework: Establish the objective: Evaluate past profitability of Amazon Prime and identify levers to improve future profitability.
Define profitability as: Revenues from Prime (membership fees + incremental sales from Prime members) minus Costs (primarily shipping costs, plus program overhead).

Assess profitability in stages of sophistication: Basic (membership fee revenue vs. shipping costs), Intermediate (net profit accounting for incremental sales uplift and higher shipping usage by Prime members), Advanced (behavioral analysis comparing Prime vs. non-Prime purchase patterns to isolate program's true net contribution).
Identify drivers of profitability: membership fee level, member count, incremental purchase frequency/volume, shipping cost per shipment, logistics efficiency.
Identify levers to improve profitability: customer segmentation, price optimization, and competitive/logistics advantage.
Prioritize analyses by impact and feasibility; clearly state what results at each step would confirm or refute the hypothesis.

questions.prompt: How would you structure the profitability assessment of Amazon Prime?
questions.guidance: Strong answers move through three layers: (1) Basic: membership fee revenue vs. direct shipping cost. (2) Intermediate: recognize Prime members buy more than non-Prime members, generating additional gross profit from incremental sales that must be weighed against their above-average shipping cost. (3) Advanced: design an analysis comparing cohort purchase behavior (frequency, basket size, category mix) of Prime vs. non-Prime customers to isolate the net economic contribution of the program. Candidate should articulate what data they would need and what outcomes would support each conclusion.

questions.prompt: What analyses would you run to identify ways to improve Prime's profitability?
questions.guidance: Three key analytical themes: (1) Customer segmentation — divide customers into 'casual' (infrequent, one-off purchases, e.g. electronics) vs. 'habitual' (frequent everyday items, e.g. household goods). Identify which segment benefits Amazon more on a net basis and devise targeted offers or services to convert casual customers to habitual ones. Proxy variables: purchase volume, frequency, category. (2) Price optimization — infer customers' willingness to pay for Prime by analyzing which customers historically enrolled at given price points. Model demand curve to find profit-maximizing annual fee. (3) Logistics/competitive advantage — assess Amazon's investments in warehouse network and inventory management that lower cost-per-shipment, creating a structural cost advantage that competitors cannot easily replicate.

brainstorming.prompt: What levers can Amazon pull to improve the profitability of the Prime program going forward?

categories.name: Revenue — Membership Pricing
ideas: Increase annual fee for new subscribers after demand analysis
Introduce tiered pricing (e.g., monthly vs. annual) to capture price-sensitive segments
Offer bundled add-ons at premium (streaming, cloud storage) to raise ARPU

categories.name: Revenue — Incremental Sales
ideas: Drive habitual purchasing through curated deals and Subscribe & Save-style prompts exclusive to Prime
Use Prime as a gateway to higher-margin private-label products
Personalized recommendations to increase basket size and frequency among casual Prime members

categories.name: Cost — Shipping Efficiency
ideas: Expand fulfillment center network to shorten last-mile distance and reduce cost per shipment
Improve inventory placement algorithms so items are already close to Prime buyers
Negotiate volume discounts with carriers; invest in Amazon Logistics (owned fleet)
Set minimum order thresholds for free shipping or introduce per-item free shipping caps

categories.name: Cost — Demand Management
ideas: Incentivize slower (standard) shipping to avoid premium express-carrier costs
Shift some shipments to Amazon Locker pickup to reduce last-mile expense
Use dynamic pricing on add-on items to offset shipping cost on low-margin orders

categories.name: Customer Mix
ideas: Target Prime marketing at habitual buyer profiles (high frequency, everyday categories)
Re-engage lapsed Prime members with targeted win-back campaigns
Analyze churn cohorts to identify at-risk members and intervene early

recommendation: Amazon Prime is likely profitable when accounting for the full picture: membership fee revenue plus incremental sales profit from the behavioral lift in Prime members' purchase frequency outweighs the elevated shipping costs they incur.

To increase profitability, Amazon should prioritize three levers: (1) price optimization based on revealed willingness-to-pay data, (2) customer segmentation to convert casual buyers into habitual buyers through targeted engagement, and (3) continued logistics investment to structurally lower per-shipment cost.
risks: If incremental sales uplift is weaker than assumed, the program may be subsidizing heavy shippers at a net loss.
Price increases risk member churn, especially among marginal/casual members; demand elasticity must be estimated carefully.
Aggressive shipping cost-cutting (e.g., minimum thresholds) could damage the customer experience that makes Prime valuable.
next_steps: Run a controlled cohort study comparing Prime vs. matched non-Prime member purchase behavior over a 12-month window to quantify true incremental revenue.
Build a price-elasticity model using historical enrollment data at different fee levels.
Benchmark per-shipment cost against industry and quantify savings from planned logistics investments.
